podcast.title: "The Metis of Mechanical Music" Article (1906)
podcast.body: In 1906, John Philip Sousa wrote an article for Appleton's magazine titled "The Metis of Mechanical Music." In it, he expressed his strong disapproval of mechanical music devices, stating that they "substitute for human skill, intelligence and soul" and predicted a "marked deterioration in American music and musical taste." "In 1906, he wrote an article for Appleton's magazine, and the title of the article was The Metis of Mechanical Music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Music vs Technology Over The Years

podcast.title: Belief in Live Music Only
podcast.body: John Philip Sousa strongly believed that music should only be experienced live. He considered the new talking machines of the turn of the 20th century, such as gramophones and phonographs that played recordings, to be "nothing short of evil." "And he believed that music was something that should only be experienced live."

srcs.episode: Music vs Technology Over The Years

podcast.title: Icon of 1890s Marching Music
podcast.body: John Philip Sousa was a prominent figure associated with marching music, which constituted the biggest form of popular music in the United States during the 1890s. His work exemplified the military music offshoot that emphasized strict time-keeping. "John Philip Suza and all that sort of thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

podcast.title: Opposition to Talking Machines
podcast.body: John Philip Sousa actively campaigned against recording technology, advocating for a ban on these machines and the recordings they played. He even appeared before the U.S. Congress to argue that talking machines would "ruin the artistic development of music in this country," and expressed concern that they would eliminate the "vocal court." "He even appeared before the U.S. Congress to make his argument. The talking machines are going to ruin the artistic development of music in this country."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Music vs Technology Over The Years

podcast.title: Prediction of Musical Deterioration
podcast.body: Sousa foresaw that recorded music would discourage people from learning music and lead to widespread unemployment among musicians. He also believed that a frozen recorded performance would become the standard, ending improvisation and evolution in music, making it "stale and boring." "I foresee a marked deterioration in American music and musical taste, an interruption of the musical development of the country and a host of other injuries to music in its artistic manifestations."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Music vs Technology Over The Years

podcast.title: Refusal to Conduct Recordings
podcast.body: For many years, John Philip Sousa proudly refused to conduct any orchestras in recording situations. He famously stated, "I have never been in the Gramophone company's office in my life," demonstrating his steadfast opposition to the recording industry until his death in 1932. "And for years, Susa refused to conduct any orchestras in any recording situations, proudly saying that I have never been in the Gramophone company's office in my life."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Theme Song from "Flying Circus" (Year not specified)
xref.body: The theme song for Monty Python's Flying Circus is actually John Philip Sousa's march, "The Liberty Bell," composed in 1893. This association made the military march widely recognizable to a new generation. "So, yeah, that's the theme from Monty Python's Flying Circus, but it's actually a march composed in 1893 by American John Philip Susa."
